Sunk cost — an already-paid cost — different concept
Marginal benefit — value of next unit — partial overlap
Public goods — jointly-consumed good — unrelated concept
questions.context: Opportunity cost is among the most important and most undertaught economic concepts. There's no free Saturday.

questions.question: A teacher offers a $50 prize to whichever of two students scores higher next week. Both study harder. Why does this work?
questions.answer: Incentives shape behavior — incentives drive behavior
choices: Incentives shape behavior — incentives drive behavior
Cash payments are illegal at most schools and the offer was theoretical — legal technicality
Incentives have no effect on behavior — a denial
Both students would study equally hard with or without the prize — inversion
questions.context: The economist's first question is always: 'what incentives does this create?' Steven Levitt's *Freakonomics* (2005) made it accessible.

questions.question: Hayek's insight: complex orders emerge from local interactions with no designer. A store has fresh February tomatoes via thousands acting independently. What's this called?
questions.answer: Spontaneous order — emergent coordination no planner
choices: Spontaneous order — emergent coordination no planner
Central planning — planner-set arrangement
Random allocation — chance distribution
Market failure — coordination breakdown
questions.context: Hayek's *Individualism and Economic Order* (1948) introduced spontaneous order. The concept extends beyond economics: language, common law, science emerge without central direction.

questions.question: On a Manhattan morning, 8M people make 30M journeys via subway, bus, walking, taxi, bike. No planner directs the flow. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Decentralized decisions coordinate outcomes no planner could match — urban-scale spontaneous order
choices: Decentralized decisions coordinate outcomes no planner could match — urban-scale spontaneous order
NY needs more central traffic-direction than any city — planning success
Traffic flow cannot exceed any planner's design without chaos — planner dependence
Traffic only works when each commuter holds an identical map — uniform-info claim
questions.context: Manhattan's daily transportation is one of the world's most complex spontaneous orders. MTA runs subway, taxis regulated — but routing, mode, timing, destination decisions are independent.

questions.question: Leonard Read's 1958 'I, Pencil' tracks a pencil to a store. Wood from Oregon; graphite from Sri Lanka; brass; rubber from Indonesia. Thousands coordinate to make one. What's the lesson?
questions.answer: No one knows how to make a pencil; pencils get made — markets coordinate knowledge
choices: No one knows how to make a pencil; pencils get made — markets coordinate knowledge
Pencils are centrally planned globally — inversion of the actual story
Pencils could be made by one craftsman alone — denying supply-chain
Pencil production requires extensive UN coordination — centralized claim
questions.context: Leonard Read's *I, Pencil* (1958) is one of the most-reprinted economic essays. Milton Friedman cited it on his 1980 *Free to Choose* PBS series.

questions.question: Buchanan and Tullock's 1962 'The Calculus of Consent' said politicians, bureaucrats, voters aren't more public-spirited than those they regulate. What field did they found?
questions.answer: Public choice theory — econ analysis of politics
choices: Public choice theory — econ analysis of politics
Behavioral economics — biases in decisions — unrelated field
Welfare economics — aggregate utility math — different concept
Game theory — strategic analysis — partial overlap
questions.context: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for public choice. The field's central move — extending self-interest analysis to political actors — collapses the 'market failure leads to government fix' framework.

questions.question: US sugar producers benefit from sugar quotas — billions in revenue. Consumers each pay a few dollars more per year. Who is more politically organized?
questions.answer: Concentrated producers — concentrated vs dispersed politics
choices: Concentrated producers — concentrated vs dispersed politics
The dispersed many (consumers) — consumers have more stake — inversion
Both groups are equally organized politically — a denial of asymmetry
Neither group cares enough to organize politically — denies the politics exists
questions.context: Sugar quotas (still in force, costing consumers billions annually) are the canonical case of concentrated benefits vs dispersed costs.

questions.question: Politicians claim policies 'serve the common good.' Public choice tells us to ask a different question first. What is it?
questions.answer: Whose specific interests does this policy serve, and at whose expense? — no policy benefits all equally
choices: Whose specific interests does this policy serve, and at whose expense? — no policy benefits all equally
How effectively does this policy serve every American? — uncritical acceptance
How many votes will this policy win in the next election? — purely electoral
What did Adam Smith say about this policy in 1776? — appeal to authority
questions.context: Public choice theory's first question: cui bono — who benefits, who pays? The 'common good' framing usually conceals concentrated beneficiaries.

questions.question: The ICC (1887) was within a decade captured by the railroads it was meant to oversee, enforcing cartel pricing. What's this called?
questions.answer: Regulatory capture — industries co-opt regulators
choices: Regulatory capture — industries co-opt regulators
Successful consumer protection — agency worked as designed
Industry rebellion against regulation — industry defied rules
Bureaucratic incompetence — agency couldn't do its job
questions.context: The ICC (1887, abolished 1995) is the textbook case of regulatory capture. Gabriel Kolko's *Triumph of Conservatism* (1963) documented how Progressive-era regulation was often welcomed by the regulated.

questions.question: A city sets strict rent control: existing rents rise 1%/year while neighborhood rents rise 5%. Existing tenants visibly benefit. What unseen costs does Bastiat's method tell us to look for?
questions.answer: Less building, less maintenance, tenant lock-in — unseen spread
choices: Less building, less maintenance, tenant lock-in — unseen spread
No real costs exist — pure landlord-tenant transfer — a no-cost claim
Higher-quality construction follows rent control — inversion of the actual effect
The federal government compensates landlords for losses — subsidy defense
questions.context: Economists across schools (Friedman, Sowell, Krugman, Stiglitz) have warned strict rent controls reduce housing supply. Textbook seen-vs-unseen.

questions.question: A minimum-wage law raises the floor from $10 to $15. Workers who keep jobs at the new wage benefit visibly. What workers does Bastiat's method tell us to look for next?
questions.answer: Hour-cut, laid-off, or unhirable workers at the higher minimum — the priced-out
choices: Hour-cut, laid-off, or unhirable workers at the higher minimum — the priced-out
Workers who immediately get promotions to manager-level positions — inversion
Federal regulators enforcing the law — a tangential effect
Workers in foreign countries whose wages also rise as a result — an irrelevant effect
questions.context: Minimum-wage debates often focus only on workers who keep jobs at the higher wage. The 'unseen' workers — priced out, can't get a first job, hours cut — are the harder-to-count loss.

questions.question: Some economists (David Card) argue minimum-wage hikes don't reduce employment as predicted. The Austrian / classical response notes one thing about most such studies. What?
questions.answer: Short-run measurements missing long-run automation substitution — dynamics matter
choices: Short-run measurements missing long-run automation substitution — dynamics matter
They're falsified by all available data — a denial of observation
They prove minimum wage has no effect on anything — over-strong reading
Consistent with Keynesian demand theory — theoretical alignment
questions.context: David Card + Alan Krueger's 1994 New Jersey-Pennsylvania study argued for limited employment effects. Critics note short time horizons, narrow industry focus, missed long-run substitution.

questions.question: Ricardo's 1817 Portugal-England wine-cloth example: both gain by specializing even when one is more efficient at both. What did Ricardo establish?
questions.answer: Comparative advantage — trade helps both, comparative
choices: Comparative advantage — trade helps both, comparative
Absolute advantage — absolute-only trade — different concept
Mercantilism — export max, import min — the doctrine Ricardo refuted
Tariff protection — raise barriers to help producers — the opposite
questions.context: Ricardo's *On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation* (1817) introduced comparative advantage. Opportunity cost matters, not absolute productivity.

questions.question: In 1930 the US passed Smoot-Hawley, raising tariffs on 20,000+ imports. Others retaliated. Global trade collapsed ~65% 1929-1934. What did Smoot-Hawley contribute to?
questions.answer: Deepening the Great Depression — worsened the catastrophe
choices: Deepening the Great Depression — worsened the catastrophe
Ending the Great Depression — tariffs protected industry
A boom in US manufacturing through the early 1930s — tariff-success story
Stabilizing global trade through enforced bilateral deals — alternative history
questions.context: Smoot-Hawley (signed June 17, 1930) is the textbook case of tariff-driven trade collapse. Over 1,000 economists signed a public petition urging Hoover to veto.

questions.question: Modern trade-protection invokes 'protecting American jobs.' Public choice and comparative advantage together suggest one move. What?
questions.answer: Identify the specific jobs being protected and the broader costs of protecting them — concentrated vs dispersed
choices: Identify the specific jobs being protected and the broader costs of protecting them — concentrated vs dispersed
Always raise tariffs to protect all American jobs equally — tariff maximization
Always cut tariffs to zero immediately — fixed prescription
Tariffs and trade have no effect on jobs in either direction — denial of any link
questions.context: Bastiat's seen-vs-unseen applied to trade: seen is the protected industry; unseen is everyone paying higher prices, exporters facing retaliation.

questions.question: Joseph Schumpeter (1883-1950, Austrian) coined 'creative destruction.' Cars beat buggy whips; phones beat film; streaming beat video stores. What's the lesson?
questions.answer: Economic progress requires obsolete businesses to fail — no new without old
choices: Economic progress requires obsolete businesses to fail — no new without old
Government must protect obsolete industries from change — the opposite of the lesson
Creative destruction is a recent phenomenon in tech only — a scope-limitation
Economic progress can occur without any business failures — denying trade-off
questions.context: Schumpeter's *Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy* (1942) introduced 'creative destruction.' Policies that 'protect jobs' often freeze the obsolete in place.

questions.question: Israel Kirzner (an Austrian who studied under Mises) emphasized the entrepreneur's distinctive economic role. What does the entrepreneur do that worker, investor, and manager don't?
questions.answer: Discovers profit opportunities others have missed — alertness to market gaps
choices: Discovers profit opportunities others have missed — alertness to market gaps
Provides labor in exchange for hourly wages — the worker role
Provides capital in exchange for interest payments — the investor role
Manages existing operations efficiently — the manager role
questions.context: Kirzner's *Competition and Entrepreneurship* (1973) distinguished entrepreneurial function from labor/capital/management. The entrepreneur spots opportunities.

questions.question: Steve Jobs returned to near-bankrupt Apple in 1997. He cut hundreds of products and focused on iMac, iPod, iPhone. Apple became one of the most valuable companies. What did Jobs do?
questions.answer: Entrepreneurial coordination toward unrecognized opportunities — the Kirznerian role
choices: Entrepreneurial coordination toward unrecognized opportunities — the Kirznerian role
Standard manager oversight of routine operations — the manager function
Labor as a salaried executive of a public company — the worker function
Passive capital investor providing financing — the capitalist function
questions.context: Jobs's return to Apple (1997-2011) combined technologies, designs, partnerships, and capital toward products consumers didn't know they wanted.

questions.question: A kid saving $5/week for 50 years at 5% returns ~$35,000 — most from compounding, not contributions. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: The 8th wonder of the world (Einstein) — compound interest engine
choices: The 8th wonder of the world (Einstein) — compound interest engine
Simple interest matches compound returns — denying compounding
Stock returns always beat bonds by exactly 5% — unrelated claim
Bonds lose value over decades — inversion of typical outcomes
questions.context: Compound interest is the most important math concept in personal finance. Saving early and letting time work is empirically more effective than saving more later.

questions.question: Inflation at 3%/year: a dollar buys ~75 cents in 10 years. At 7%/year (post-2020): ~50 cents. What does inflation do to dollar savers?
questions.answer: Imposes a hidden tax on saved purchasing power — inflation transfers savers to issuers
choices: Imposes a hidden tax on saved purchasing power — inflation transfers savers to issuers
Rewards savers by automatically increasing nominal dollar amounts — inversion of the effect
Has no effect on purchasing power if wages keep up — wage-indexation defense
Creates new wealth for everyone equally across the economy — denying Cantillon
questions.context: Inflation is the regressive wealth-transfer Bastiat would spot instantly. Seen: nominal dollar amounts. Unseen: their purchasing power erodes.

questions.question: A person can borrow at 6% for a car or save at 5% in a bond. Opportunity cost matters: borrowing pays interest; saving foregoes. What's the economic concept?
questions.answer: Time preference — present-vs-future trade-off
choices: Time preference — present-vs-future trade-off
Marginal cost — marginal unit cost — unrelated concept
Public choice — econ of politics — unrelated concept
Spontaneous order — emergent coordination — unrelated concept
questions.context: Time preference is foundational to Austrian capital theory (Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's *Capital and Interest* in three volumes 1884-1909).

questions.question: A teen sees identical shoes at two stores: $60 vs $80. Same brand, same model, same condition. The teen drives to the cheaper store. What economic concept did the teen use?
questions.answer: Arbitrage — choosing low when the same good has two prices
choices: Arbitrage — choosing low when the same good has two prices
Public choice — economic analysis of political incentives — unrelated
Aggregate demand — total spending on goods and services — unrelated
Marginal product — output from one more unit of input — unrelated
questions.context: Arbitrage drives prices toward consistency across markets. In well-functioning markets, identical goods converge in price; persistent gaps signal frictions (transport, taxes, regulation).

questions.question: A small bakery raises bread prices from $4 to $5. Customers grumble but most keep buying because the alternative bakery is across town. The owner's revenue rises despite some lost sales. What concept describes this?
questions.answer: Inelastic demand — quantity demanded falls only a little when price rises
choices: Inelastic demand — quantity demanded falls only a little when price rises
Elastic demand — quantity falls sharply with any price rise — the opposite case
Zero demand — no one buys at any price — not applicable here
Infinite demand — unlimited buying regardless of price — not applicable here
questions.context: Demand elasticity measures responsiveness of quantity to price. Bread is fairly inelastic (necessity); luxury items are more elastic. Inelasticity gives producers more pricing power.

questions.question: In 2008 US housing crashed; in March 2020 stocks crashed before rallying. Investors who panicked at the bottom locked in losses; those who held recovered. What concept does this show?
questions.answer: The danger of selling at the bottom — crashes feel permanent but markets historically recover
choices: The danger of selling at the bottom — crashes feel permanent but markets historically recover
Markets always go up forever with no risk — too optimistic
Markets always go down forever with no recovery — too pessimistic
Government always rescues investors in crashes — sometimes, not always
questions.context: Behavioral finance research (Kahneman, Thaler, Shiller) shows investors systematically buy high and sell low. Long-term wealth-building requires resisting the urge to panic at market bottoms.

questions.question: Across these concepts (prices, opportunity cost, public choice, spontaneous order, comparative advantage), what's the unifying insight?
questions.answer: Economic systems coordinate dispersed information no individual could possess — the Hayekian thread
choices: Economic systems coordinate dispersed information no individual could possess — the Hayekian thread
Economic systems are best designed by experts using sophisticated math — a different framework
Economic systems are random and cannot be analyzed at all — denial of analytical economics
Economic systems work the same way as physics systems — methodology equivalence
questions.context: The Hayekian thread — that prices encode dispersed knowledge no individual possesses — connects supply/demand, marginal analysis, time preference, public choice, spontaneous order.

questions.question: Bastiat's 1850 'Seen and Not Seen' uses a broken window. Seen: glazier's work. Unseen: everything else the shopkeeper would have bought. What broader method does this teach?
questions.answer: Always look for second-order effects, trade-offs, costs not in the immediate picture — economic thinking
choices: Always look for second-order effects, trade-offs, costs not in the immediate picture — economic thinking
Always count only the visible effects of a policy — opposite of Bastiat
Always defer to expert opinion on economic policy — appeal to authority
Always support free-trade agreements without analysis — fixed prescription
questions.context: Bastiat's method (see what's not visible) is the bank's signature voice. It applies to every policy question.

questions.question: Free-market economists (Sowell, Hayek, Friedman, Mises) keep returning to one core question on any policy. What is it?
questions.answer: What do people do when they're free to choose? — revealed preferences are data
choices: What do people do when they're free to choose? — revealed preferences are data
What do politicians prefer at the moment? — deferral to authority
What do mathematical models predict aggregate outcomes? — model-centric approach
What does academic consensus say about the policy? — an appeal to authority
questions.context: Free-market economists trust revealed preferences over stated preferences. Policy respecting revealed preferences tends to outperform.

questions.question: Milton Friedman said 'no free lunch.' Heinlein coined it (1966); Friedman made it economics. What's the lesson?
questions.answer: Every benefit has a cost — someone pays even if hidden
choices: Every benefit has a cost — someone pays even if hidden
Government can produce benefits at zero cost when properly organized — inversion of the lesson
Lunches at restaurants are free under certain promotional conditions — literal reading
Some benefits in economics are genuinely costless to all parties involved — a denial
questions.context: 'No free lunch' applies to subsidies (taxpayers pay), tariffs (consumers pay), regulations (compliance), printing money (savers pay through inflation).
